patients.summary: Administrative assistant with long-standing lupus on prednisone 15 mg, type 2 diabetes on metformin and glargine, and diet-managed hypertension who joins in 2018. Endocrinology diagnoses Cushing syndrome in 2020, lisinopril starts in 2021, insulin is cut for early-morning lows in 2023, and she has a left frontal ischemic stroke in November 2025 treated with tenecteplase, leaving mild word-finding trouble.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
43 y/o woman establishing care. Left her prior primary office after repeated turnover; wants one doctor who knows her.

HISTORY
- Lupus (SLE) for years, managed by an outside rheumatology group. Has been on prednisone 15 mg every morning long term; rheum writes it. Joints and skin quiet lately per pt.
- Type 2 diabetes for years. Metformin 1000 twice a day and a glargine pen 24 units at night. Checks sugars most mornings, usually 130s-150s, no lows she can recall.
- Blood pressure has run a little high at prior visits; told to cut salt and walk, never put on a pill.
No surgeries.

MEDS: metformin 1000 mg BID; insulin glargine 24 units qHS; prednisone 15 mg qAM.
ALLERGIES: none to medications.
FAMILY: mother has type 2 diabetes. Father has high blood pressure. Maternal grandmother had cerebrovascular disease.
SOCIAL: married. Works as an administrative assistant. Never a smoker. A glass or two of wine in a week, socially. 

ROS: no chest pain, dyspnea, edema, rash, joint swelling, polyuria, vision change.

EXAM: BP slightly above goal today, other vitals as recorded. Well appearing. Skin without rash. Oropharynx clear. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Joints without synovitis. Feet: intact monofilament bilaterally, pulses 2+, skin intact.

A/P
1. T2DM on metformin + basal insulin, long-term prednisone likely contributing. A1c, CMP, urine albumin/creatinine today. Eye exam is due, she will book with her optometrist.
2. Elevated BP, no meds. Recheck at each visit; home cuff suggested.
3. SLE on chronic prednisone, rheum managing. Will request their notes.
4. Health maintenance: Tdap given. One-time hep C and HIV screen sent. Lipids today. Will review the prior office's Pap and mammogram once records come.
Follow up 4-5 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Adriana, your labs from Tuesday are back. The A1c is 7.9, which is above where we'd like it (under 7 is the usual target), not unexpected on daily prednisone. Kidney and liver tests are fine, the urine protein screen is normal, and blood counts are normal. Cholesterol: LDL is about 100. The hepatitis C and HIV screens were both negative. We'll recheck the A1c in the fall. Nice to finally have you here.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: MA
documents.body:
Received 38 pages from her previous primary care office, scanned to media. Abstracted for the PCP:
- Pap with HPV co-test 2016: negative for intraepithelial lesion, HPV negative.
- Screening mammogram 2017: BI-RADS 1, negative.
- Problem list there: diabetes type 2, lupus (rheum), elevated BP.
- Meds there match what pt brought. No drug allergies.
- Last eye exam noted 2016, no retinopathy.
Rheumatology letters not included; separate request faxed to the rheum group.

documents.title: Office Visit: fatigue, weight gain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
First in-person visit since winter.

S: Over roughly the last six months she has felt more and more worn out, and stairs have gotten hard; she pulls on the railing to get up to the second floor. Up about 20 lb since spring though she says she is eating the same and moving about the same. Bruises from bumping into things she doesn't remember. Periods have become irregular this year. No fever, chest pain or dyspnea. Prednisone still 15 mg daily, no dose bursts this year per her.

O: weight up about 9 kg from last November. BP above goal. Face rounder than at her prior visits. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.

A/P:
1. Weight gain, proximal weakness, bruising, menstrual change on long-term prednisone. Concern for Cushing syndrome. CBC, CMP, TSH today. Referring to endocrinology for evaluation.
2. T2DM, A1c will come with the endocrine workup, sugars higher at home lately.
3. BP higher, will revisit once endocrine has weighed in.
Flu vaccine given today.

documents.title: Labs and endocrinology referral
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Adriana, the blood count, kidney and liver tests, potassium and thyroid test from Wednesday are all normal, so thyroid isn't the explanation for the weight and tiredness. The endocrinology referral is in; their office should call you within a couple of weeks. Let me know if you don't hear.

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology, consultation of 11/19/2020 (received by fax 01/12/2021 after records request).

Reason for referral: possible hypercortisolism.

History: 45-year-old woman with SLE on long-term prednisone, type 2 diabetes and hypertension. For about half a year she has been progressively tired and has struggled with stairs. She has put on roughly 20 lb without a change in eating or activity, bruises easily, and her cycles have become irregular.

Medications: metformin 1000 mg twice daily; insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime; prednisone 15 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: mother with type 2 diabetes; father hypertensive; maternal grandmother with cerebrovascular disease.
Social: administrative assistant, never smoker, 1-2 glasses of wine weekly.

Examination: round, full face. Fat pads above both clavicles. Skin thin and fragile. Proximal muscle strength 3/5 in shoulders and hips bilaterally; distal strength preserved.

Results: 8 AM serum cortisol 28 mcg/dL (ref 6-23). 24-hour urine free cortisol 350 mcg/24 h (ref 20-90). ACTH 22 pg/mL (ref 9-52). Fasting glucose 160 mg/dL. Hemoglobin A1c 7.8%.

Assessment: Cushing syndrome, clinically and biochemically, in a patient receiving chronic glucocorticoid therapy for lupus. Diabetes above target.

Recommendations: glucocorticoid dosing to be reviewed with her rheumatologist, who manages her lupus. Continue current diabetes regimen for now. Return to endocrinology clinic for follow-up.

Thank you for this referral.

documents.title: Endocrinology appointment
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi Doctor, I saw the endocrinologist a couple of weeks ago. She said my tests show Cushing syndrome and that it's from the cortisol being too high. She said she'd talk to my rheumatologist about the prednisone. Did you get her letter? I didn't really understand everything.

documents.title: RE: Endocrinology appointment
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for telling me, Adriana. We don't have their letter yet. Our office will request it today, and once I've read it I'll go over it with you. In the meantime keep taking your prednisone exactly as prescribed; it should never be stopped suddenly.

documents.title: Rheumatology follow-up letter
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
Outside rheumatology group, visit 02/22/2021.

Dear colleague,
Ms. Pagan returns for her lupus and for monitoring of long-term immunosuppressive therapy with prednisone. We note endocrinology's diagnosis of Cushing syndrome three months ago.

She describes brief dizziness now and then when she stands up quickly. No chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations. Her glucose log looks moderately controlled on metformin.

Blood pressure in clinic was 152/96 and her pulse ran mildly fast. No jugular venous distension, lungs clear without crackles, no peripheral edema. Joints quiet, no rash.

Renal function on our monitoring labs is stable. The baseline transthoracic echocardiogram done 02/10 showed preserved systolic function with no wall motion abnormalities (report enclosed).

Assessment: SLE, clinically quiet. Long-term current use of an immunosuppressant (prednisone 15 mg daily), continued. Blood pressure above goal; we would be grateful if you would address antihypertensive therapy.

Medications: prednisone 15 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime. NKDA.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Blood Pressure Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen after rheum's letter flagged BP 152/96. Home cuff 140s-150s/90s most days for a month.
Exam: BP still up today, recorded. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema.

A/P: Hypertension, now persistently above goal with diabetes and on steroids. Time to treat. Starting lisinopril 10 mg daily. Explained how it works in plain terms: it blocks a hormone that squeezes the blood vessels down, and in people with diabetes it also helps protect the kidneys. Possible dry cough, dizziness; stand up slowly. BMP and BP check in two weeks.

Two weeks on lisinopril. Home numbers better, mostly low 130s/80s. Gets a little lightheaded if she jumps up from her desk fast; passes within a few seconds. No falls, no swelling, no chest pain, energy no worse. No cough.
Exam: BP improved today. Heart regular. No edema.
Plan: continue lisinopril 10. Rise slowly. BMP today to check potassium and kidney function. Next diabetes visit in the fall unless home readings change.

documents.title: Endocrinology follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology, clinic visit 05/24/2023 (received 08/09/2023 in response to records request).

Interval history: Ms. Pagan returns for Cushing syndrome and type 2 diabetes. She has kept to her eating plan and her walking. For several weeks she has woken many mornings drenched in sweat with her heart pounding. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no recent illness.

Medications reviewed: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime, lisinopril 10 mg daily, prednisone 15 mg daily. NKDA.
Family and social history unchanged: never smoker, social wine, administrative assistant.

Exam: BP 132/84, HR 78, BMI 29. General examination unremarkable.

Labs today: hemoglobin A1c 6.2%; fasting plasma glucose 72 mg/dL; creatinine 1.0 mg/dL; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 25 mg/g.

Assessment:
1. Severe hypoglycemia: recurrent early-morning episodes on basal insulin, with A1c now well below target for her.
2. Type 2 diabetes.
3. Cushing syndrome on chronic glucocorticoid for lupus; steroid management remains with rheumatology.

Plan: reduce insulin glargine to 20 units at bedtime. Glucagon 1 mg kit prescribed; husband to be shown how to use it. Check fingerstick before bed and on waking for two weeks. Return in one year or sooner if lows persist.

documents.title: Insulin change
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, just letting you know the endocrinologist lowered my night insulin from 24 to 20 because I've been waking up sweaty with my heart racing, she said my sugar is dropping too low early in the morning. She also gave me a glucagon shot to keep at home. Should I change anything else?

documents.title: RE: Insulin change
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for the update. Follow her new dose of 20 units. Nothing else changes for now. Check your sugar at bedtime and when you wake for the next couple of weeks, and for any reading under 70 take 15 grams of fast sugar (4 oz juice) and recheck in 15 minutes. Make sure your husband knows where the glucagon is. We'll get her note.

Annual. Feels OK. Weight has crept up again this year. No lows at all since spring 2023.

2. T2DM, A1c today. Hypoglycemia from 2023 resolved after dose change; removing from active list.
3. HTN on lisinopril, controlled.
4. Prevention: flu today, COVID in a few weeks. Mammogram December. Shingrix once she turns 50 in February.

Dear colleague, annual review for SLE. She has had no flares. Denies joint swelling, photosensitive rash, ulcers or pleurisy. Exam without synovitis or rash. Our monitoring blood count, metabolic panel and urinalysis were normal. Disease quiet; prednisone 15 mg daily continued. Follow-up one year.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department, 11/22/2025 (copy received 11/28/2025).

CC: confusion and slurred speech, about two hours.

HPI: 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, Cushing syndrome and lupus on chronic prednisone, with an episode of severe hypoglycemia in 2023. Her husband drove her in after she abruptly became muddled and her words came out garbled around midday. She takes her medicines as prescribed: metformin, insulin glargine 24 units at night, lisinopril 10 mg, prednisone 15 mg. NKDA. Never smoker, social wine.

Exam: BP 155/90, P 88, T 36.8 C. Awake and alert. Aphasic. Right lower facial droop. Right arm weak. 

Workup: glucose 180 mg/dL, so hypoglycemia is not the explanation. HbA1c 7.8%. Platelets and INR normal. Noncontrast head CT: no hemorrhage, no mass effect.

Course: stroke team activated. Within the treatment window, no contraindication identified; risks and benefits reviewed with patient and husband. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus given. Repeat neuro checks every 15 minutes, no worsening. Her husband and then her sister, who arrived later, asked for updates; both were updated with the patient's agreement.

Impression: acute ischemic stroke.
Disposition: admitted to the stroke unit.

medications.drug: aspirin 81 MG Delayed Release Oral Tablet

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth at bedtime

reports.text: MRI brain without contrast, including diffusion-weighted imaging. Small focus of restricted diffusion with corresponding low ADC signal in the left frontal lobe within the left middle cerebral artery territory, consistent with acute infarct. No hemorrhage on susceptibility imaging. No mass effect. Ventricles normal in size. No other acute abnormality.
reports.conclusion: Small acute left frontal (left MCA territory) infarct. No hemorrhage.

reports.text: Bilateral carotid duplex. Common, internal and external carotid arteries patent with normal waveforms. Velocities within normal limits bilaterally. Vertebral arteries antegrade.

Left ventricle normal in size with normal systolic function and no regional wall motion abnormality. Normal right ventricle. No intracardiac thrombus. Agitated saline study without shunt seen. Valves without significant disease. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Normal LV size and function. No thrombus. No shunt seen.

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Regional hospital, stroke unit. Admitted 11/22/2025, discharged 11/25/2025. (Received 12/08/2025.)

Diagnosis: acute ischemic stroke, left frontal (left MCA territory), treated with IV tenecteplase.
Other problems: type 2 diabetes on insulin; hypertension; Cushing syndrome; SLE on chronic prednisone.

Course: arrived via the ED with aphasia, right facial droop and right arm weakness about two hours after onset; head CT without hemorrhage; tenecteplase given. No neurological worsening and no bleeding complication. MRI the next morning showed a small acute left frontal infarct without hemorrhage. Carotid duplex without significant stenosis. Echocardiogram with normal LV function, no thrombus and no shunt seen on bubble study. Telemetry throughout the stay showed sinus rhythm with no atrial fibrillation. Aspirin started 24 hours after thrombolysis once repeat imaging was clear. High-intensity statin started. Blood pressure allowed to run higher in the first day, then lisinopril increased. Insulin and prednisone continued at home doses; glucose 140s-190s.

At discharge: speech much improved with mild word-finding difficulty; right arm strength nearly back to normal; walking independently.

Discharge medications: aspirin 81 mg daily (new); atorvastatin 80 mg nightly (new); lisinopril 20 mg daily (increased from 10 mg); metformin 1000 mg twice daily; insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime; prednisone 15 mg daily; glucagon kit as needed. NKDA.

Follow-up: primary care within 1 week; outpatient speech therapy (referral placed); stroke neurology clinic in about 10 weeks. No driving until cleared by neurology.

documents.title: Call from husband
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pt's husband called (pt on speaker, gave permission). She had a stroke Saturday, got the clot-busting medicine in the ED, now in the hospital stroke unit, talking better already. Expected home in a day or two. Scheduled post-hospital visit 12/1 with PCP. Asked them to bring the discharge papers and all bottles. PCP aware.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen with her husband, 6 days after discharge from the stroke unit. Discharge summary not yet received; reviewed the patient's discharge paperwork and the pharmacy fill history.

S: Talking much better; sometimes stops mid-sentence hunting for a word. Right arm feels normal to her. No headache, new weakness, vision change or bleeding. Speech therapy evaluation is booked for next week. Not driving. Her sister has been helping during the day.

Meds reconciled from bottles and pharmacy: aspirin 81 daily (new), atorvastatin 80 nightly (new), lisinopril 20 daily (up from 10), metformin 1000 BID, glargine 24 qHS, prednisone 15 daily, glucagon kit. Old lisinopril 10 bottle set aside.

O: BP at goal today. Alert, fluent with occasional word-finding pauses, follows commands. Face symmetric at rest. Strength 5/5 and equal in arms and legs. Gait normal. Heart regular, lungs clear. PHQ-9 4.

A/P:
1. Acute ischemic stroke, left frontal, s/p tenecteplase: improving. Continue aspirin and high-intensity statin. Speech therapy. Neuro clinic follow-up in February. No driving until neurology says so. Reviewed stroke warning signs, call 911.
2. HTN: lisinopril 20, BP at goal.
3. T2DM: A1c 7.8 in hospital. Same insulin for now; recheck in January with lipids and liver tests on the new statin.
4. Mood: PHQ-9 low, will keep checking.
5. Work: will complete FMLA paperwork for time off.

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Speech therapy twice a week, says her therapist is pleased. Word-finding pauses less often. No new neuro symptoms. Tolerating atorvastatin, no muscle aches. Aspirin, no bleeding. Fasting 130s-150s, no lows.
O: BP at goal. Speech fluent with rare pauses. Strength symmetric. Heart regular, lungs clear.
A/P: post-stroke, improving. Lipids, CMP, A1c today. Neuro clinic in February. Continue current meds. Diabetes visit in April.

documents.title: January results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Adriana, the LDL cholesterol dropped to 58 on the atorvastatin, which is where we want it after a stroke. Liver tests are normal on the statin. A1c is 7.9, higher than I'd like; diet over the holidays and less walking likely played a part. We'll recheck in April before changing insulin. Glad the speech therapy is going well.

documents.title: Stroke clinic follow-up
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Outside stroke neurology clinic, visit 02/11/2026.

Ms. Pagan returns about 11 weeks after a small left frontal ischemic stroke treated with tenecteplase. Her speech has improved substantially with therapy; she notices an occasional pause to find a word, mostly when tired. No new focal symptoms.

Exam: fluent speech with rare word-finding hesitation; comprehension, repetition and naming intact. Cranial nerves normal, face symmetric. Strength 5/5 throughout, normal tone, reflexes symmetric. Sensation and coordination normal. Gait normal.

Assessment: recovering well from left MCA territory ischemic stroke, mild residual word-finding difficulty.
Plan: continue aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 80 mg. Blood pressure and diabetes per primary care. Cleared to drive. Finish the current speech therapy course. Follow up as needed.
Medications reviewed: aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril 20 mg, metformin, insulin glargine 24 units, prednisone 15 mg. NKDA.

A/P:

2. HTN at goal on lisinopril 20.

Pap/HPV due this year, will do at September visit. Mammogram overdue since December, order sent.
